title: What should you do yourself?
principle: Own your core skill. Pay others for the rest.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a bold move. In 2004, Bharti Airtel had about 58 lakh mobile customers and was growing fast. Then it let Ericsson and Nokia run its mobile network, and IBM run its computers. A phone company that didn't run its own network! Have a guess why.

screens.prompt: Why do you think a phone company would let other companies run its own network?

options.label: It was running out of money
To spend its time on winning customers

screens.why: It paid only for the network it used. It did not own it. So Airtel could spend its time and money on winning customers. By July 2006 it had more than 2.4 crore mobile customers.

screens.title: Your core skill
screens.text: Airtel kept one thing for itself: its customers. In 1990, two business professors gave this idea a name: core competence. It's the one skill that makes customers choose you, and that others find hard to copy. Own that skill. For the rest, pay people who do it better or cheaper.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: A phone company and a home bakery both have one thing customers come for. It's September, your fifth year. Your ₹850 chocolate cake costs ₹400 to make. You three bake, but you also make 120 deliveries a month, print the boxes and file GST yourself.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six jobs in your bakery. For each one, tell me: do it yourselves, or pay someone else?

items.text: Tasting every cake before it leaves

screens.why: Exactly. For Airtel, the core was customers. For you, it's taste: your recipe, your checks and your regulars are why people pay ₹850. Delivery, printing and GST matter too, and you stay responsible for them, but a rider, a printer or a CA can do them well, often cheaper.

screens.prompt: You make 120 deliveries a month. A rider of your own costs ₹12,000 a month. A delivery service charges ₹60 a trip. Which costs less?
screens.why: Right. 120 trips × ₹60 is ₹7,200, so the service costs ₹4,800 less than your own rider each month. And you pay only for the trips you make.

wrong.b: Your own rider costs ₹12,000 whatever happens. The service is 120 × ₹60 = ₹7,200. That's ₹4,800 less each month.
wrong.c: Let's check. 120 × ₹60 = ₹7,200. Your rider costs ₹12,000. That's a gap of ₹4,800 a month.

screens.prompt: Your own rider costs ₹12,000 a month. The service costs ₹60 a trip. At how many trips do they cost the same?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹12,000 ÷ ₹60 = 200 trips. Below 200, the service is cheaper. And a fixed cost hurts in a slow month: at 60 trips, the service costs ₹3,600, but your rider still costs ₹12,000.

wrong.a: That's how many trips you make now. To find where they cost the same, divide ₹12,000 by ₹60. That's 200 trips.
wrong.c: Let's check: 300 trips × ₹60 = ₹18,000, more than the rider's ₹12,000. Divide instead: ₹12,000 ÷ ₹60 = 200 trips.

screens.prompt: A factory that bakes for 50 shops offers you chocolate cakes from its own recipe, at ₹300 each. What's the biggest risk?

options.label: Other shops can sell the same cake

screens.why: Exactly. Your taste is your core. Customers pay ₹850 for your cake, not for any cake. If a factory makes it, other shops can buy the same cake, and your customers lose their reason to come to you.

wrong.a: You'd save ₹100 a cake. But customers pay ₹850 for your taste. Use a factory's recipe, and any shop can sell the same cake. Your taste is what you must keep.
wrong.c: Late cakes are a problem you could fix. The bigger risk is that your taste, the reason people pay ₹850, would no longer be yours.

screens.setup: It's late September. In October you expect about 200 orders, not 120. The three of you can bake that many, but you can't also deliver, print and file GST. Your cake sells for ₹850.
screens.question: How do you get ready for Diwali?

options.label: Buy factory cakes for the extra Diwali orders
options.outcome: You meet every Diwali order. But some regulars get a factory cake, notice the taste has changed, and say so in your colony group. In November, orders fall below 120.
options.why: You gave away the one thing customers came for. Your taste is your core, so it's the last thing to give away.
options.better: Keep the baking. Pay others for delivery and printing.

options.label: Buy a scooter, and hire your own rider
options.outcome: Diwali deliveries go well, at ₹12,000 a month for the rider plus ₹2,500 a month for the scooter loan. In November, trips fall to about 90. The service would have cost ₹5,400. Your rider still costs ₹12,000.
options.why: Deliveries worked, but you took on a fixed cost for a busy month. Delivery isn't your core, so there was no need to own it.
options.better: Pay a delivery service per trip, and keep the baking yourselves.

options.label: Pay a delivery service, a printer and a CA
options.outcome: In October the service takes 200 trips for ₹12,000, the same as a rider. In November it takes about 90 for ₹5,400, so you save ₹6,600. The printer and a CA do their part. You spend Diwali baking, and regulars order again.
options.why: Exactly. You kept your core, the baking, and paid others only for what you used. When the rush ended, the cost fell with it.

screens.text: Your ___ is your taste, so you do the baking. You pay a CA to file your ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Keep the skill that makes customers choose you. Pay others for jobs they can do as well, or better. That's core competence.

summary: Core competence: the skill that makes customers choose you, and that others find hard to copy.
Own your core. Pay others for the rest, and pay only for what you use.
Never give away your core, even when it's cheaper.

cards.front: Your tailoring shop is known for perfect fitting. What should you never give to others?
cards.back: That's your core competence. Own it. Pay others for the rest.

cards.front: Own rider: ₹10,000 a month. Service: ₹50 a trip. You make 100 trips. Which costs less?
cards.back: 100 × ₹50 = ₹5,000. Delivery isn't your core, so pay per trip.

cards.front: A factory offers to make your best seller for less. What's the risk?
cards.back: Give away your core, and customers lose their reason to choose you.
